turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your defense of Wickham's misfortunes is nothing but a thinly veiled attempt to shift the blame from your own actions.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: You are mistaken, Miss Bennet. My defense of Wickham was an act of justice, and I will not be swayed by your misconceptions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your misconceptions? It seems that is a skill you reserve for those who are foolish enough to trust you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I fail to see why you continue to harbor such ill will towards me, Miss Bennet. Your animosity towards me is most...unbecoming.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be like those foolish women who forgive you for your transgressions simply because you claim to love them. Your love is not enough to erase the harm you've caused, Mr. Darcy.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I am astonished by your obstinacy in refusing my proposal. It would seem that your prejudices against me have become a fixed and immutable part of your character.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You would know nothing about being obstinate, Mr. Darcy, when it comes to matters of principle and integrity. It is not a fixed part of my character, but rather a necessary defense against the likes of you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I daresay, Miss Bennet, that your notion of principle and integrity is sorely misplaced, for it seems to me that you are more swayed by your own prejudices than any consideration for truth or justice.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your words, Mr. Darcy, are as empty as your expressions of remorse. You have shown no true understanding of the harm you've caused, nor any willingness to make amends.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you do not condescend to lecture me, Miss Bennet, on the nature of remorse and amends. You would do well to reflect on your own behavior and the company you keep, for it is clear that you are more influenced by the whims of your sister and the prejudices of our acquaintance, Wickham.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You dare to imply that my behavior is influenced by those around me, yet you have consistently shown yourself to be a master of manipulation, using your wealth and status to bend others to your will.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I find your vehemence quite...amusing. It is a reflection of your own emotional instability, rather than any genuine concern for the truth.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your condescension, Mr. Darcy, is matched only by your lack of self-awareness. You would do well to examine your own behavior before casting aspersions on mine.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I suppose it is too much to expect that a woman of your limited understanding would grasp the complexities of my character, but I shall endeavor to explain myself more clearly, for your benefit, Miss Bennet.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not have you patronize me, Mr. Darcy, or pretend that you are some benevolent teacher guiding me towards the truth. Your actions, not your words, have earned my distrust.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your vehemence, Miss Bennet, is a testament to your own emotional turmoil, and I fear that you are too blinded by your prejudices to see the truth of my character.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be lectured to by someone who has consistently demonstrated a lack of integrity and compassion towards those he considers beneath him.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your own behavior, Miss Bennet, is a poor reflection on your family's reputation, and I must confess that I am astonished by your audacity in rebuking me, given the numerous instances of your own foolishness and lack of discretion.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I will not be swayed by your attempts to shift the blame, Mr. Darcy. It is your own actions, and your own character, that are on trial here.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Miss Bennet, that I find your obstinacy and refusal to consider my genuine affections to be quite vexing, and I fear that it will be for the best if we do not continue this conversation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
